SK1041 Use a compound assignment

An assignment whose right-hand side is a binary operation on the assignment target itself, where the compound operator says it once.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

Naming the target twice is the shape a rename can half-finish: total = subtotal + 1 compiles and is a different program, and nothing in the long form says which of the two occurrences was meant. The compound form cannot drift, and it is the form C# has had since version 1 — the long one is what a model writes because most of its training data predates the habit.

Example

Instead of:

count = count + 1;

Write:

count += 1;

When it does not fire

The direction is safe and the reverse is not: C# defines x op= y as x = (T)(x op y) with an explicit conversion back to the target's type, which the long form lacks — byte b; b = b + 1; does not compile at all, so the rule never sees the shapes where the conversion differs. A cast on the right-hand side is therefore never unwrapped: long l; l = (int)(l + 1); truncates and l += 1 does not. Only whole expression statements are reported, the target must be a chain of plain names, and the binary operator's left operand must be that same target textually — which excludes x = x + a + b, whose left operand is x + a. && and || have no compound spelling and are excluded. Comments and preprocessor directives between the target and the operator are excluded because the fix deletes that text. ⚠ #423: the receiver of the target must run no code. The long form evaluates it twice and the compound form once, so h.Current.X = h.Current.X + 5 over a counting getter is declined — the audit measured two reads before and one after. The last link may be any property, because its getter and setter each run once in both forms. A C# 14 instance operator += is declined too: the compound form is bound speculatively and must resolve to the binary operator's own method, which is why the rule is now semantic. ⚠ Inside an argument a [CallerArgumentExpression] parameter captures (Debug.Assert on .NET 9+, ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull, test asserts) the rewrite changes the captured string, so the finding's fix is not marked safe there — #422 decides it in the host, per call site, and this rule's executable fixture pins it. With that and #423's guard, every executable fixture's Probe is unchanged and the fix is safe again.
